flawed_step: Step 1: by Rédei's theorem, T has a Hamiltonian path v1→v2→v3→v4. This step is justified. Step 2: close the path into a cycle using the arc v4→v1. This step cannot be justified. The pair {v1,v4} may be joined by v1→v4 instead, and no reordering of the path helps unless T is strongly connected (Camion's theorem). A general 4-vertex tournament need not be strongly connected.
counterexample: The transitive tournament on vertices {1,2,3,4} has the arc i→j exactly when i<j: 1→2, 1→3, 1→4, 2→3, 2→4, 3→4. Each of the 6 pairs gets exactly one arc, so this is a tournament. Every arc goes from a smaller label to a larger one. Along any directed walk the labels strictly increase, so no walk can return to where it started. So T has no directed cycle at all, and in particular no Hamiltonian cycle. Another way to see it: vertex 1 has in-degree 0, so no cycle can pass through it.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. A tournament has a Hamiltonian cycle only if it is strongly connected. The transitive tournament on 4 vertices (i→j exactly when i<j) is acyclic: vertex 1 is a source with in-degree 0. So it has no Hamiltonian cycle. The proof attempt breaks when trying to close the Hamiltonian path into a cycle.
